blocks.text: The National Essential Medicines List (NEMLIT) identifies the medicines considered essential for managing priority health conditions at all levels of the healthcare system. NEMLIT is grounded in the World Health Organization’s (WHO) concept of essential medicines—those that address the population’s most critical health needs, are consistently available within a functioning health system, and meet standards of quality while remaining affordable to both individuals and the community. This approach relies on a careful, evidence-based selection process that evaluates safety, efficacy, and comparative cost- effectiveness. Limiting the list to essential medicines helps strengthen supply chains, promote rational use, and reduce overall healthcare costs.

The previous edition of the Standard Treatment Guidelines introduced the classification of antibiotics into Access, Watch, and Reserve (AWaRe) categories to promote optimal antibiotic use and address antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

runs.text: and Reserve (AWaRe) categories to promote optimal antibiotic use and address antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

blocks.text: The National AWaRe List 2025 was developed using Tanzania’s AMR, antimicrobial use (AMU), and antimicrobial consumption (AMC) surveillance data from 2020–2023, together with research evidence from 2014–2024. The list classifies 70 antibiotics, compared with 54 in the 2020 list, and is incorporated into the seventh edition of the STG/NEMLIT to guide rational antibiotic use, support antimicrobial stewardship, mitigate AMR, and improve patient outcomes.

blocks.text: Access antibiotics: First- or second-line treatment options for common infections with relatively lower resistance potential. They should be widely available and account for more than 60% of total antibiotic use.

blocks.text: Watch antibiotics: Antibiotics with a higher resistance potential that should be used cautiously and for specific indications. Their use should account for ≤28% of total antibiotic use.

blocks.text: Reserve antibiotics: Last-resort antibiotics for confirmed or strongly suspected multidrug-resistant infections. Their use should, whenever feasible, be guided by culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing and account for ≤12% of total antibiotic use. The AWaRe classification provides a framework for monitoring antibiotic use, improving access to essential antibiotics, promoting appropriate prescribing and preserving the effectiveness of critical antimicrobial agents.

As observed in Sixth Edition of the STG/NEMLIT 2021, the NEMLIT has been assigned with levels of healthcare facilities and level of expertise, which guides the stocking and prescribing of medicines to facilitate ordering from Medical Stored Department (MSD) and reimbursement by the National Health Insurance Funds (NHIF).

blocks.text: These guidelines indicate three levels of the healthcare system, which includes Primary, Secondary and Tertiary level of care. The Primary level comprises Dispensaries denoted by letter (A), Health Centers denoted by letter (B) and Council/District Hospitals denoted by letter (C), while the Secondary level includes Regional Referral Hospitals denoted by letter (D) and the Tertiary level, which consists of Zonal, Special and National Hospitals denoted by letter (S).

blocks.text: Additionally, these guidelines recognize the prescriber’s level of expertise in relation to medicine prescribing, regardless of the level of the healthcare facility. This means that a prescriber may, based on their professional qualification, prescribe medicines appropriate to their level of expertise even when working in a facility classified at a level lower than his /her level of expertise, provided that approval has been granted by the Ministry following verification confirming the presence of the expert at that facility (the approval procedure is outlined in the Note:2 box below). For example, if a specialist is stationed at a dispensary, he or she may be authorized to prescribe Level S medicines in accordance with the guidelines.

blocks.text: Under these guidelines, prescribing authority is aligned with the level of professional expertise. Specialists, denoted by (A, B, C, D & S), are authorized to prescribe all medicines listed in the STG/NEMLIT. Medical Officers, indicated by (A, B, C & D), may prescribe medicines assigned to those levels, while Assistant Medical Officers, denoted by (A, B & C), are permitted to prescribe medicines within those categories. Clinical Officers, indicated by (A & B), are limited to prescribing medicines classified under Levels A and B, and Assistant Clinical Officers, denoted by (A), are authorized to prescribe only medicines categorized under Level A.
